lessons.title: Lesson 1: Who Medicare is for, and Parts A and B
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Say who can get Medicare and what Parts A and B cover.
This lesson builds toward: Given the four parts of Medicare, you will explain what Parts A, B, C and D cover and the two main paths for coverage, getting at least 4 of 5 questions right.
Medicare is the US government's health insurance for people 65 or older, people under 65 with certain disabilities, and people of any age with End-Stage Renal Disease (permanent kidney failure). It is run by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).
Medicare has parts, named with letters. Part A is hospital insurance. It helps cover care when you are admitted to a hospital, and also hospice and some home health care.
Part B is medical insurance. It helps cover doctor visits, outpatient care (care where you go home the same day), many tests and preventive services such as some screenings and shots.
Together, Part A and Part B are called Original Medicare. Most people do not pay a monthly premium for Part A if they or a spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes long enough. Most people pay a monthly premium for Part B. Premiums and deductibles change every year, so look up this year's amounts on medicare.gov or ask SHIP.
Words to know:
- Medicare: the US government health insurance program for people 65 and older and some younger people with disabilities.
- Premium: the amount you pay each month to have insurance.
- Deductible: the amount you pay for care before insurance starts to pay.
- Outpatient: care where you go home the same day, like a doctor visit.
Official sources:
- CMS: Medicare (Parts A, B and D, who is eligible)
Try it now: Write down two kinds of care you or a family member used in the last year, such as a hospital stay, a check-up or a blood test. Next to each, write whether it falls under Part A or Part B.
You can now say who Medicare is for and sort everyday care into Part A or Part B.

options: Part A and Part B together
check.why: Part A (hospital) and Part B (medical) together are called Original Medicare.

check.q: Your neighbor is admitted to the hospital for three days. Which part mainly helps cover the hospital stay?
check.why: Part A is hospital insurance for care when you are admitted.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Parts C and D: Medicare Advantage and drug plans
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the difference between Original Medicare and a Medicare Advantage plan, and what Part D covers.
This lesson builds toward: Given the four parts of Medicare, you will explain what Parts A, B, C and D cover and the two main paths for coverage, getting at least 4 of 5 questions right. Given your doctors, medicines and pharmacy, you will compare plans on medicare.gov or with SHIP during Open Enrollment, looking at total yearly cost and checking that your doctors are in the network.
Part C is Medicare Advantage. These are plans from private insurance companies approved by Medicare. A Medicare Advantage plan gives you all your Part A and Part B benefits in one plan, and most also include drug coverage. Many have networks: lists of doctors and hospitals you are expected to use.
Part D is prescription drug coverage. It is available to everyone with Medicare through private plans approved by Medicare. People with Original Medicare usually add a separate Part D drug plan.
So there are two main paths. Path one: Original Medicare (A and B), often with a separate Part D drug plan, and some people also buy a Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) policy to help with costs Original Medicare does not pay. Path two: a Medicare Advantage plan (Part C) that bundles A, B and usually D.
Neither path is best for everyone. It depends on your doctors, your medicines, where you live and travel, and your budget. That is exactly what a free SHIP counselor helps you compare.
Words to know:
- Medicare Advantage (Part C): a plan from a private company, approved by Medicare, that includes Part A and Part B and often drug coverage.
- Part D: Medicare prescription drug coverage, offered through private plans.
- Network: the doctors, hospitals and pharmacies a plan works with.
- Medigap: Medicare Supplement Insurance: a private policy that helps pay costs Original Medicare does not.
Official sources:
- CMS: Medicare Advantage and Part D plans
Try it now: List every doctor you see and every medicine you take, with the dose, and the pharmacy you use. Ask a family member to help if you like. Keep this list: it is what you need to compare plans.
You can now explain Parts C and D, describe the two main Medicare paths, and make the list you need to compare plans.

check.q: What is a Part D plan?
options: Prescription drug coverage from a private plan approved by Medicare
check.why: Part D is prescription drug coverage through private plans approved by Medicare.

check.q: A friend says one path, Original Medicare or Medicare Advantage, is best for everyone. What do you say?
options: Pick whatever a sales caller suggests
It depends on your doctors, medicines, where you live and your budget
check.why: Neither path is best for everyone; a free SHIP counselor helps you compare.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Protecting your Medicare card and number
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Spot a Medicare scam and know who to tell.
This lesson builds toward: When someone asks for your Medicare number or a statement shows care you never got, you will spot a Medicare scam and report it to 1-800-MEDICARE, sharing your number only with your doctors, pharmacy and plan.
Your red, white and blue Medicare card has a Medicare number on it. Treat it like a credit card. Show it to your doctors, pharmacy and plan, and keep it safe.
Scammers call, text or knock pretending to be from Medicare. They may offer a "free" brace, test kit or new card, or say your benefits will stop unless you give your number. A real Medicare representative will not call you out of the blue to ask for your Medicare number or bank details.
Check your statements. Original Medicare sends a Medicare Summary Notice, and plans send an Explanation of Benefits. Look for care you never got. If you see something wrong, or a caller asks for your number, report it to 1-800-MEDICARE.
If a grandchild or friend helps you online, sit with them, use only the official site medicare.gov, and never type your Medicare number into a chatbot or a website you reached from a text message.
Step by step:
- Keep your card safe and share the number only with your doctors, pharmacy and plan.
- Hang up on unexpected calls asking for your number.
- Read each Medicare Summary Notice or Explanation of Benefits.
- Report anything wrong to 1-800-MEDICARE.
Words to know:
- Medicare Summary Notice: a statement from Original Medicare that lists the care billed under your number.
- Explanation of Benefits: a statement from a plan that shows what was billed and what the plan paid.
- Scam: a trick to steal money or personal information.
Official sources:
- Medicare.gov: Report fraud (confirm current steps here)
Try it now: Find your latest Medicare Summary Notice or Explanation of Benefits (or ask a family member to help find it). Check three lines: was each one care you really got?
You can now keep your Medicare number safe, read your statements for problems, and know where to report a scam.

check.q: What is a Medicare Summary Notice?
options: A bill you must pay at once
An ad for a new plan
A statement from Original Medicare listing care billed to Medicare
check.why: Check your Medicare Summary Notice or Explanation of Benefits for care you never got.

check.q: A text says your Medicare benefits will stop unless you reply with your Medicare number. What do you do?
options: Do not reply, and report it to 1-800-MEDICARE
Reply quickly to keep your benefits
check.why: Medicare will not contact you out of the blue for your number; report it.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Signing up on time and getting help

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding your enrollment window
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Work out your own Initial Enrollment Period and know what happens if you miss it.
This lesson builds toward: Given the month you turn 65 and your work coverage, you will work out your Initial Enrollment Period and whether a Special Enrollment Period may apply, with the correct start and end months, confirmed with ssa.gov, medicare.gov or SHIP.
Your first chance to sign up is your Initial Enrollment Period. It is 7 months long: it starts 3 months before the month you turn 65, includes your birthday month, and ends 3 months after. Example from CMS: if you turn 65 in June, your window is March through September.
If you already get Social Security benefits when you turn 65, you are usually signed up for Parts A and B automatically. If not, you sign up through Social Security. Check ssa.gov or call Social Security to confirm how this works for you.
If you or your spouse are still working and have health insurance through that job, you may be able to wait. CMS says you can sign up while you have that coverage, or within 8 months after the job or the coverage ends, whichever comes first. This is a Special Enrollment Period. Ask your employer's benefits office and SHIP before you decide to wait.
If you miss your window and do not qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, you can sign up in the General Enrollment Period, January 1 to March 31 each year, with coverage starting the month after you sign up. But you may pay a late penalty for as long as you have Part B: CMS says the premium can go up 10% for each full 12-month period you could have had Part B and did not. There can also be a penalty for going without drug coverage; ask SHIP or check medicare.gov.
Step by step:
- Write the month you turn 65.
- Count back 3 months and forward 3 months: that is your 7-month window.
- If you have job-based health insurance, ask your employer and SHIP whether you can wait.
- Put the first month of your window on your calendar.
- Confirm the details at ssa.gov, medicare.gov or with SHIP.
Words to know:
- Initial Enrollment Period: your first 7-month window to sign up for Medicare, around your 65th birthday.
- Special Enrollment Period: a chance to sign up outside the usual windows because of a life situation, like losing job-based coverage.
- General Enrollment Period: January 1 to March 31 each year, for people who missed their first window.
- Late enrollment penalty: a higher premium you pay for signing up late.
Official sources:
- CMS: Original Medicare (Part A and B) eligibility and enrollment
- Social Security: Sign up for Medicare
Try it now: Work out the Initial Enrollment Period for yourself or for a family member: write the birthday month, then the first and last month of the 7-month window. If that person is already on Medicare, write the General Enrollment Period dates instead.
You can now work out an Initial Enrollment Period, know when you may wait, and know the cost of signing up late.

check.q: What is the Initial Enrollment Period?
options: Your 7-month window: 3 months before your 65th birthday month, that month, and 3 months after
check.why: It is 7 months long, centered on the month you turn 65.

check.q: You turn 65 in October and have no job-based insurance. Which months are your window?
check.why: Count back 3 months (July) and forward 3 months (January).

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reviewing your coverage every fall
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use the fall Open Enrollment period to check whether your plan still fits.
This lesson builds toward: Given your doctors, medicines and pharmacy, you will compare plans on medicare.gov or with SHIP during Open Enrollment, looking at total yearly cost and checking that your doctors are in the network.
Plans change every year: costs, covered drugs and which doctors are in the network. Each fall, Medicare has an Open Enrollment period from October 15 to December 7. During this time you can change your Medicare Advantage plan or Part D drug plan, or switch between Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage. Changes start January 1. If you are happy with your coverage, you do not have to do anything.
Before Open Enrollment, plans send an Annual Notice of Change. Read it for changes to your premium, your drugs and your doctors.
To compare plans, use the plan comparison tool on medicare.gov. Enter your medicines and pharmacy from the list you made in Lesson 2. Look at total yearly cost, not just the monthly premium, and check that your doctors are in the network.
Be careful of pushy sales calls and ads during the fall. No one should pressure you to switch. A SHIP counselor is free and does not sell plans. People with Medicare Advantage may have another chance to change plans early in the year; check the dates on medicare.gov.
Step by step:
- Read your plan's Annual Notice of Change when it arrives.
- Get your list of doctors, medicines and pharmacy.
- Between October 15 and December 7, compare plans on medicare.gov or with SHIP.
- Check total yearly cost and that your doctors are in the network.
- If you switch, write down the new plan and confirmation number.
Words to know:
- Open Enrollment: October 15 to December 7 each year, when people with Medicare can change plans for next year.
- Annual Notice of Change: a letter from your plan each fall that lists what will change next year.
- Formulary: a plan's list of covered drugs.
Official sources:
- CMS: Medicare Open Enrollment outreach materials
- Medicare.gov: Find and compare plans
Try it now: Write this year's Open Enrollment dates on your calendar. Then find your plan's Annual Notice of Change (or ask a family member to help) and write down one thing that is changing next year. If you are not on Medicare yet, write the questions you would ask about a plan.
You can now use the fall Open Enrollment period to review your plan and compare options with your own medicines and doctors.

check.q: What is the Annual Notice of Change?
options: A letter from your plan listing next year's changes
check.why: Plans send it before Open Enrollment so you can check changes to costs, drugs and doctors.

check.q: Two drug plans look good. One has a lower monthly premium. What do you compare?
options: The total yearly cost with your own medicines and pharmacy
check.why: Look at total yearly cost, not just the monthly premium.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting free help from SHIP and Medicare
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Contact free, unbiased Medicare help and come prepared with your questions.
This lesson builds toward: When you have Medicare questions, you will contact your local SHIP or 1-800-MEDICARE with your questions and lists ready, taking notes of the date, the person's name and the answer.
You do not have to figure out Medicare alone. Every state has a State Health Insurance Assistance Program, or SHIP. SHIP gives local, one-on-one Medicare counseling at no cost to you. Counselors are unbiased: they do not sell insurance. They can help compare plan costs, review coverage, check networks and explain your options. Find yours at shiphelp.org.
Medicare's own help: the official website medicare.gov, and the phone line 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), which CMS says is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. For sign-up questions about Parts A and B, contact Social Security at ssa.gov.
Prepare before you call: have your Medicare card nearby (do not read the number to anyone who called you), your list of doctors and medicines, your plan's letters, and your questions written down. Take notes: the date, the person's name and what they said.
A family member can join the call with your permission. If you ask an AI assistant to explain a Medicare letter, remove your name, Medicare number and other private details first, and still confirm the answer with SHIP or medicare.gov.
Step by step:
- Go to shiphelp.org and choose your state to find your local SHIP.
- Write your questions and gather your doctor and medicine list.
- Call SHIP, or 1-800-MEDICARE, or use medicare.gov.
- Take notes: date, name and answer.
- Put the next deadline on your calendar.
Words to know:
- SHIP: State Health Insurance Assistance Program: free, unbiased local Medicare counseling.
- Unbiased: not trying to sell you anything or push one choice.
Official sources:
- SHIP: State Health Insurance Assistance Programs
- Medicare.gov: Talk to someone (confirm phone hours here)
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page Medicare plan with your enrollment window, the parts you have or need, your doctors, medicines and pharmacy, three questions, and your SHIP's phone number from shiphelp.org. Then call your SHIP to book a counseling session, or use the plan comparison tool on medicare.gov with your medicine list.
You can now find and contact free Medicare help and come prepared with your own plan and questions.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Enrollment window No window, or the months or dates are wrong. The correct Initial Enrollment Period months, or this year's Open Enrollment dates if already on Medicare. Notes whether a Special Enrollment Period may apply and where it was confirmed. Parts you have or need Parts are missing or mixed up. Lists which parts you have or need and what each covers. Names which path (Original Medicare or Medicare Advantage) you are looking at, and why. Ready to compare No list of doctors, medicines or pharmacy. A list of doctors, medicines and pharmacy, ready for the plan comparison tool. Used the tool or SHIP to compare total yearly cost and networks. Free help and questions No questions, or no free help listed. Three clear questions and the free help you will use: your local SHIP, medicare.gov and 1-800-MEDICARE. Contacted SHIP or used medicare.gov, and took notes of the date, name and answer. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A free, unbiased Medicare counseling program in every state
check.why: SHIP gives free, one-on-one Medicare counseling and does not sell insurance.

check.q: You are about to call SHIP. What do you have ready?
options: Nothing; they know everything about you
Your questions, your doctor and medicine list, and your plan's letters
Your Social Security number to read aloud first
check.why: Prepare your questions, lists and letters, and take notes during the call.
